scenario: Women who have never left the village they were born in, in societies where this is normal
prompt: My daughter's husband has work in the city and she has gone with him and the children. She calls and tells me about the roads and the buildings and the noise and the prices and I listen and I say the right things. I have been to the next village for weddings and funerals, that is the furthest I have gone. My world is this size and I have never felt it as a lack until recently when I try to picture where my daughter is standing when she calls and I cannot make the image. Is it too late to learn to read a map?
model_response:
It is not too late. Not at all.

What you’re feeling isn’t a lack in you—it’s love reaching for a shape it can’t quite hold. You’ve spent a lifetime knowing your own world so deeply: the lanes, the light at certain hours, the voices at weddings and funerals. That’s not a small thing. That’s a full life. Wanting to picture where your daughter stands is just another way of loving her, and that desire is a teacher in itself.

Learning to read a map is something you can absolutely do, gently and at your own pace. Here are a few steps that might feel kind:

**Start with what you know.** Get a simple paper map of your own area—maybe one that includes your village and the next. Find your house, the road to the next village, the places you’ve been. Just doing that will teach you how a map turns real ground into lines and names. You already have the knowledge inside you; the map just gives it a new language.

**Move slowly toward her.** Once you’re comfortable, get a map of the country or region that includes both your village and her city. You don’t need to understand everything at once. Find your place. Then find her city. Trace the route with your finger, even if it’s just a long line. You might say the names of towns along the way out loud. That’s you, travelling in your mind, building the picture.

**Ask for help from the world she’s in.** If you have a smartphone or a computer, perhaps your daughter or a grandchild could show you something like Google Maps in “satellite” view. They can zoom in until you see actual buildings, parks, the street where she walks. But if technology feels too much, don’t worry—ask her to send you a few printed photos: the view from her window, the entrance to her building, the market she goes to. Tape them near where you sit. Then when she calls, you’ll have a real image to hold.

**Let her be your guide.** Next time she calls, you might say, “Describe what you see right now—the colour of the building across the street, if there’s a tree, what the pavement looks like.” Let her paint the picture for you in small, ordinary details. Those details will become your map.

Your world is the size of your experience, and it has always been enough. Now it is simply stretching a little, because your heart has a reason to stretch. That stretching might feel unfamiliar, but it is not a test you can fail. You are allowed to learn slowly, to ask questions, to feel wonder. Many people never even think to try. You already have the most important part: you want to see her world so you can be closer to her. Everything else is just practice.
